{{smaller block|The prisoner brought several persons of good credit to ''witness'' to her reputation.
{{right|''Addison'', Tatler, No. 259.}}}}

'''2†.''' To take witness or notice.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Witnesse'' on him, that any perfit clerk is,
That in scole is gret altercacioun
In this matere and greet disputisoun.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Nun’s Priest’s Tale, l. 416.}}}}
'''Witnessing clause.''' Same as ''testatum.''

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To give testimony to; testify; bear witness of, or serve as evidence of; attest; prove; show.
{{smaller block|<poem>We purchace, thurgh oure flateryng,
Of riche men of gret pouste,
Lettres to ''witnesse'' oure bounte.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 6958.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>For I ''witnesse'' you, and say in thys place
That he was a trew catholike person.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1529.}}}}
{{smaller block|Behold how many things they ''witness'' against thee.
{{right|Mark xv. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Methought you said
You saw one here in court could ''witness'' it.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', All’s Well, v. 3. 200.}}}}
{{smaller block|For what they did they had custom for; and could produce, if need were, testimony that would ''witness'' it for more than a thousand years.
{{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim’s Progress, i.}}}}
{{smaller block|[''Witness'' in this sense is often used in the subjunctive imperatively or optatively, in many cases with inversion.
<poem>Heaven ''witness'',
I have been to you a true and humble wife.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., ii. 4. 22.}}}}

A willow of any species. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|<poem>See where another hides himself as sly
As did Actæon or the fearful deer,
Behind a ''withy''.</poem>
{{right|''J. Dennys'' (Arber’s Eng. Garner, I. 170).}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''Withy'' is a reasonable large tree (for some have been found ten feet about). {{right|''Evelyn'', Sylva, i. 20.}}}}
'''2.''' A withe; a twig; an osier.
{{smaller block|<poem>With grene ''wythyes'' y-bounden wonderlye.</poem> {{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 58.}}}}
{{smaller block|A kind of oblong vessel made of bark, by the simple contrivance of tying up the two ends with a ''withy''.
{{right|''Cook'', First Voyage, iii. 8.}}}}
'''3.''' A halter made of withes.—'''4.''' In ''ceram.'', same as ''twig''<sup>1</sup>, 3.—'''Gray withy''', {{smaller|the sallow or goat willow, ''Salix caprea''.}}—'''Hoop withy.''' {{smaller|Same as ''hoop-withe''. See ''Rivina''.}}

'''withy<sup>2</sup>''' (with′i or wī′ᴛ̵ʜi), ''a.''   [< ''withe'', ''with''<sup>2</sup>, + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Made of withes; like a withe; flexible and tough.
{{smaller block|<poem>I learnt to fold my net, . . .
And ''withy'' labyrinths in straits to set.
{{right|''P. Fletcher'', Piscatory Eclogues, i. 5.}}

Thirsil from ''withy'' prison, as he uses,
Lets out his flock.
{{right|''P. Fletcher'', Purple Island, iii.}}</poem>}}

'''withy-pot†''' (with′i-pot), ''n.'' A vessel or nest of osiers or twigs.
{{smaller block|There were ''withy-potts'' or nests for the wild fowle to lay their eggs in, a little above y<sup>e</sup> surface of y<sup>e</sup> water.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Feb. 9, 1665.}}}}

'''withywind†''' (with′i-wīnd), ''n.'' Same as ''withwind''.   ''Minsheu.''
{{smaller block|Whiter Galet then the white ''withie-winde''.
{{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., p. 521.}}}}

'''witjar†''' (wit′jär), ''n.''   [< ''wit''<sup>1</sup> + ''jar''<sup>3</sup>, ''n.'']   The head; the brainpan; the skull. [Old slang.]
{{smaller block|Dr. Hale, who was my good Astolfo (you read Ariosto, Jack), and has brought me back my ''wit-jar'', had much ado . . . to effect my recovery.
{{right|''Richardson'', Clarissa Harlowe, V. cxxxiii.}}}}

'''witless''' (wit′les), ''a.''   [Also formerly or dial. ''weetless''; < ME. ''witles'', < AS. *''witleás'' (in deriv. ''witleást'') (= Icel. ''vitlauss''), witless: as ''wit''<sup>1</sup> + ''-less.'']    '''1.''' Destitute of wit or understanding; thoughtless; unreflecting; stupid.
{{smaller block|<poem>But, man, as thou ''witlees'' were,
thou lokist euere dounwarde as a beest.</poem>
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 185.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Raymounde semede all ''witlese'' to deuise,
All merueled that gan it aduertise.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2846.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And ''weetlesse'' wandered
From shore to shore emongst the Lybick sandes,
Ere rest he fownd.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. 9. 41.}}}}
{{smaller block|A witty mother! ''witless'' else her son.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., ii. 1. 266.}}}}
'''2.''' Not knowing; unconscious. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Smiling, all ''weetless'' of th’ uplifted stroke,
Hung o’er his harmless head.</poem>
{{right|''J. Baillie.''}}}}
'''3.''' Proceeding from thoughtlessness or folly; not under the guidance of judgment; foolish; indiscreet; senseless; silly.
{{smaller block|Fond termes, and ''witlesse'' words.
{{right|''Spenser'', Shep. Cal., July.}}}}
{{smaller block|Youth, and cost, and ''witless'' bravery.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., i. 3. 10.}}}}

'''witlessly''' (wit′les-li), ''adv.'' In a witless manner; without the exercise of judgment; without understanding.   ''Beau. and Fl.''

'''witlessness''' (wit′les-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being witless; want of judgment, understanding, or consideration.
{{smaller block|Wilful ''witlessness.''
{{right|''Sir E. Sandys'', State of Religion.}}}}

'''witling''' (wit′ling), ''n.''   [< ''wit''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ling''<sup>1</sup>.]   A pretender to wit; a would-be wit. {{smaller block|<poem>A beau and ''witling'' perish’d in the throng.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', R. of the L., v. 59.}}}}
{{smaller block|Newspaper ''witlings.''
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Retaliation, Postscript.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''witlings'' of Bath, constantly buzzing about him [Mr. Quin] to catch each accent falling from his tongue in order to pass it current for their own, were not content with robbing him of his wit, but more than once attacked his reputation. {{right|''Life of Quin'' (reprint 1887), p. 52.}}}}

'''witloof''' (wit′lōf), ''n.''   [D., lit. ‘white-leaf.’]   A variety of chicory with large roots, and forming a close head of leaves like that of a Cos lettuce. {{smaller|In Brussels these heads are cooked as a dinner-vegetable. Witloof is less bitter than the common chicory, and forms an equally good winter salad; its thick stubby root also is as good as the ordinary for mixing with coffee. Also called ''large-rooted Brussels chicory''.}}

'''witmonger''' (wit′mung″gėr), ''n.'' One who deals or indulges in wit of a poor or low kind; a witling.   ''Wood'', Athenæ Oxon.

'''witness''' (wit′nes), ''n.''   [< ME. ''witnesse'', ''witnisse'', < AS. ''witnes'', also ''ge-witnes'' (= MD. ''wetenisse'' = OHG. ''gewiznessi''), testimony, < *''witen'', orig. pp. of ''witan'', know, or rather of ''wītan'', see, + ''-nes'', E. ''-ness'': see ''wit''<sup>1</sup> and ''-ness''. Cf. ''forgiveness'' for *''forgivenness''.]   '''1.''' Testimony; attestation of a fact or event; evidence: often with ''bear'': as, to ''bear witness''.
{{smaller block|<poem>If he aske as for more ''witnesse'',
Who sent to hym and how that I hym knewe,
Telle hym it is his sone Generydes.</poem>
{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S), l. 2382.}}}}
{{smaller block|If I ''bear witness'' of myself, my ''witness'' is not true.
{{right|John v. 31.}}}}
{{smaller block|Heaven and thy thoughts are ''witness''.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., ii. 6. 32.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''witness'' of the Wapentake is distinctly against the claimant.
{{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Norman Conquest, V. 518.}}}}

'''2.''' One who or that which bears testimony or furnishes evidence or proof.

{{smaller block|Laban said, This heap is a ''witness'' between me and thee this day.
{{right|Gen. xxxi. 48.}}}}
{{smaller block|Your mother lives a ''witness'' to that vow.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iii. 7. 180.}}}}
{{smaller block|These, opening the prisons and dungeons, cal’d out of darknesse and bonds the elect Martyrs and ''witnesses'' of their Redeemer.
{{right|''Milton'', Apology for Smectymnuus.}}}}

'''3.''' One who is personally present and sees some act or occurrence, or hears something spoken, and can therefore bear witness to it; a spectator.

<poem>Neither can I rest
A silent ''witness'' of the headlong rage,
Or heedless folly, by which thousands die.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Cowper'', Task, iii. 218.}}}}

'''4†.''' A sponsor, as at a baptism or christening.

{{smaller block|He was ''witness'' for Win here—they will not be called godfathers—and named her Win-the-fight.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Bartholomew Fair, i. 1.}}}}

'''5.''' In ''law'': (''a'') One who gives testimony on the trial of a cause; one who appears before a court, judge, or other officer, and is examined under oath or affirmation. (''b'') One whose testimony is offered, or desired and expected. (''c'') One in whose presence or under whose observation a fact occurred. (''d'') One who upon request by or on behalf of a party subscribes his name to an instrument to attest the genuineness of its execution: more exactly, an ''attesting witness'' or a ''subscribing witness''.

<poem>He bad hym goo and in no wise to fayle
To the Sowdon, and telle hym the processe,
And he wold be on of his cheff ''witnesse''.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1509.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>
Is it not
A perfect act, and absolute in law,
Sealed and delivered before ''witnesses,''
The day and date emergent?
</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson,'' Staple of News, v. 1.}}}}
'''6.''' In ''bookbinding,'' an occasional rough edge on the leaf of a bound book, which is a testimony that the leaves have not been unduly trimmed. [Eng.]—'''Auricular, credible, intermediate witness.''' {{smaller|See the adjectives.—'''Hostile witness,''' a witness who manifests a disposition to injure the case of the party by whom he is called. The party is allowed in such a case to put leading and searching questions such as he could not otherwise put to his own witness, and to contradict his testimony more freely.—'''Second-hand witness.''' See ''second-hand''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To impeach a witness.''' See ''impeach.''—'''Ultroneous witness.''' See ''ultroneous.''—'''With a witness†,''' with great force, so as to leave some mark as a testimony behind; to a great degree; with a vengeance.}}
{{smaller block|This, I confess, is haste, ''with a witness.'' {{right|''Latimer.''}}}}
{{smaller block|Here ’s packing, ''with a witness!''
{{right|''Shak.,'' T. of the S., v. 1. 121.}}}}

'''witness''' (wit′nes), ''v.''   [< ME. ''witnessen, witnissen, wytnessen;'' < ''witness, n.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To bear witness or testimony; give evidence; testify.
{{smaller block|And the storye of Noe ''wytnessethe,'' whan that the Culver broughte the Braunche of Olyve that betokend Pes made betwene God and Man. ''Mandeville,'' Travels, p. 11.
The men of Belial ''witnessed'' against him, even against Naboth, . . . saying, Naboth did blaspheme God and the king. {{right|1 Ki. xxi. 13.}}}}

{{smaller block|The prisoner brought several persons of good credit to ''witness'' to her reputation.
{{right|''Addison'', Tatler, No. 259.}}}}

'''2†.''' To take witness or notice.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Witnesse'' on him, that any perfit clerk is,
That in scole is gret altercacioun
In this matere and greet disputisoun.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Nun’s Priest’s Tale, l. 416.}}}}
'''Witnessing clause.''' Same as ''testatum.''

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To give testimony to; testify; bear witness of, or serve as evidence of; attest; prove; show.
{{smaller block|<poem>We purchace, thurgh oure flateryng,
Of riche men of gret pouste,
Lettres to ''witnesse'' oure bounte.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 6958.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>For I ''witnesse'' you, and say in thys place
That he was a trew catholike person.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1529.}}}}
{{smaller block|Behold how many things they ''witness'' against thee.
{{right|Mark xv. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Methought you said
You saw one here in court could ''witness'' it.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', All’s Well, v. 3. 200.}}}}
{{smaller block|For what they did they had custom for; and could produce, if need were, testimony that would ''witness'' it for more than a thousand years.
{{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim’s Progress, i.}}}}
{{smaller block|[''Witness'' in this sense is often used in the subjunctive imperatively or optatively, in many cases with inversion.
<poem>Heaven ''witness'',
I have been to you a true and humble wife.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., ii. 4. 22.}}}}
{{smaller block|Pilgrims should watch, . . . but, for want of doing so, ofttimes their rejoicing ends in tears, and their sunshine in a cloud; ''witness'' the story of Christian at this place.
{{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim’s Progress, ii.]}}}}

'''2.''' To show by one’s behavior; betray as a sentiment.

{{smaller block|Capt. Dekings, an anabaptist and one that had ''witnessed'' a great deal of discontent with the present proceedings.
{{right|''Pepys'', Diary, Apr. 15, 1660.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Long mute he stood, and, leaning on his staff,
His wonder ''witness’d'' with an idiot laugh.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Cym. and Iph., l. 112.}}}}

'''3.''' To see or know by personal presence; be a witness of; observe.

{{smaller block|This is but a faint sketch of the incalculable calamities and horrors we must expect, should we ever ''witness'' the triumphs of modern infidelity.
{{right|''R. Hall.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>What various scenes, and O! what scenes of woe,
Are ''witnessed'' by that red and struggling beam!</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., vi. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|My share of the gayety consisted in ''witnessing'' the daily appareling of Eliza and Georgianna, and seeing them descend to the drawing-room dressed out in thin muslin frocks and scarlet sashes, with hair elaborately ringleted.
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Jane Eyre, iv.}}}}

'''4.''' To see the execution of and affix one’s name to (a contract, will, or other document) for the purpose of establishing its identity: as, to ''witness'' a bond or a deed.—'''5.''' To foretell; presage; foretoken. [Rare.]

<poem>Ah, Richard, . . .
I see thy glory like a shooting star
Fall to the base earth from the firmament!
Thy sun sets weeping in the lowly west,
''Witnessing'' storms to come, woe, and unrest.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., ii. 4. 22.}}}} ={{sc|Syn.}} '''3.''' ''Perceive, Observe'', etc. See ''see''<sup>1</sup>.

'''witness-box''' (wit′nes-boks), ''n.'' The inclosure in which a witness stands while giving evidence in a court of law.

'''witnesser''' (wit′nes-ėr), ''n.''   [< ''witness'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who gives or bears testimony.
{{smaller block|A constant ''witnesser'' of the passion of Christ.
{{right|''T. Martin'', Marriage of Priests.}}}}

'''witnessfully†''' (wit′nes-fu̇l-i), ''adv.''   [ME. ''wytnessefully''; < ''witness'' + ''-ful'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.]   By witnesses; with proof; manifestly; publicly.
{{smaller block|In this wyse more clerly and more ''wytnessefully'' is the office of wise men i-treted.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, iv. prose 5.}}}}

'''witness-stand''' (wit′nes-stand), ''n.'' The place where a witness, while giving evidence in court, is stationed.

'''witsafe†''', ''v. t.'' See ''withsafe''.

'''wit-snapper†''' (wit′snap″ėr), ''n.'' One who affects repartee.
{{smaller block|Goodly Lord, what a ''wit-snapper'' are you!
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., iii. 5. 55.}}}}

'''witstand†''' (wit′stand), ''n.''   [< ''wit''<sup>2</sup> + ''stand'', ''n.'']   The state of being at one’s wits’ end; hence, a standstill. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|They were at a ''witstand'', and could reach no further.
{{right|''Bp. Hacket'', Abp. Williams, i. 188. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''wit-starved''' (wit′stärvd), ''a.'' Barren of wit; destitute of genius. [Rare.] (''Imp. Dict.'')

'''wittal<sup>1</sup>†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''witwall.''

'''wittal<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' See ''wittol''<sup>1</sup>.

'''witte†''', ''n.'' An obsolete spelling of ''wit''<sup>1</sup>.

'''witted''' (wit′ed), ''a.''   [< ''wit''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.]   Having wit or understanding: commonly used in compounds, as quick-''witted'', slow-''witted'', etc.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
